utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 17th of March, 2010. I would like to greet everyone in the courtroom, especially Mr. Coric, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Prlic. I would also like to greet the two accused who are not in the courtroom for various reasons. I would also like to greet the counsels. I would like to greet Mr. Bos, Mr. Scott, and their fellow workers, and everyone assisting us around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would also like to greet our witness, Colonel Andabak, who is already in the courtroom. I will give the floor to the Registrar, who has IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted their lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Milivoj Petkovic. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC01203. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit IC01204. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC01205. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit IC01206. And the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit IC01207. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. The cross-examination will carry on through the Praljak Defence. Mr. Kovacic, you have given us three additional documents. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's carry on from where we left off yesterday. And the binder that you received yesterday is the thick binder. 2D1367 is the number, and I think it's the fourth document in order. Now, we were talking yesterday about the fact that the military police battalions -- or, rather, I mean on Monday; I meant to say "on Monday," anyway, that the VP battalions, military police battalions, didn't act independently as an army, but when the need arose, they were re-subordinated to the army. Now take a look at this order, and we're talking about the summer of 1993. The date is the 28th of July. And look at the introductory sentences: "The forces of the military police, apart from their -- or in addition to their duties, are engaged with the HVO forces in combat action, and so there would be no further misunderstanding, I command:" And then it goes on to say, in very precise terms, that these are cases where we see that all the military police units and forces are being attached to the HVO forces until the assignment is carried out, and that they are subordinate to the HVO, that is to say, the army. And item 2 clearly states that: "MP forces in this case shall perform tasks given to it by the HVO commander." And in item 3 it is clearly stated that the one of the purposes of this order is to do -- so that there should be no more misunderstanding between the commanders of the HVO and the military police. Now, my question to you is as follows: This principle as stated here, the principle of subordination [as interpreted] of the military police units, that they are subordinated [as interpreted] to the army -- to combat units, is that it; does this say at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Defence counsel, that's it, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now take a look at the next document, the one immediately after this one, which is composed of two documents, in actual fact, or two versions of the same document, if you will. And it is P03068. The first version is the Paket link, but it is a very poor copy, and we see all the stamps there, the official stamps, but I'm going to read the original on the basis of which the first one was compiled. So this is the second copy, which is more legible. So this is a minor case, not terribly important, but the principle is the same. On the 1st of July, 1993, Mr. Valentin Coric -- may we zoom down, please, for the English - is sending a document. He is referring to it as reply to a request, and he's sending it to the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina and the commander of the military police platoon which it concerns, and he says very clearly here that a military police platoon commanded by a certain man named Perica Turalija, which is on assignment in Prozor, and so on and so forth, until otherwise recalled, is placed under the OZ command and will be used in the carrying out of combat assignments in the Prozor area. Now, tell me, did you know this man Perica Turalija, whose mentioned here, at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I did know the platoon commander, Perica Turalija, and he was the commander of the platoon attached to the 3rd Company of the Active-Duty Military Police unit under the command of the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that from this document it clearly follows that the platoon commanded by Perica Turalija, and now I'm going to use a colloquial term, he was re-subordinated, but let me use a colloquial term and say that he was lent to the operative zone for a certain period of time, because it says "until the unit is recalled," is that right, until the explicit order is revoked?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, since he was already in Prozor, it means that he was directly placed under the command of the commander of the operative zone until this was revoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this re-subordination, as I said in my introduction when I asked you my first question, can be determined by the execution of a certain task or assignment or by a time-period that can be limited in time, such as, in this case, there's a dead-line; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's skip the next document, which is 4010 -- or let's take a brief look at it. It's a short document and confirms what we've just been saying. Could you just take a look at it? It is P4010, 4010, which is the next document in line, and it's also a small order dated August 1993, and it is addressed to you, in actual fact. And from it, it follows that -- well, I'm particularly interested in item 2. Item 1 is a description. Item 2 says: "The unit shall be under the direct command of the commander of the city of Mostar Defence, Mr. Mijo Jelic." So when your light assault battalion was sent to Mostar, it was being sent to Mostar and it was being subordinated to Jelic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, this order relates to subordination again, the subordination of a unit. And here it says that the unit shall be under the direct command of the command of the city of Mostar, and we did, in fact, report to the commander of the defence of Mostar, but the commander of Mostar was, in fact, the commander of the operative zone, and we acted within the frameworks of the operative zone, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's take a look at the next document in that same set, linked to the same topic, which is P3778. This is a document written towards the end of July 1993, so roughly the same period, and there are more details here. We could read through all of them, but I'm just actually interested in one point here, so I'll focus on that. It was, again, an order for re-subordination, and it says explicitly in the first paragraph that the unit should be re-subordinated to the HVO command or the command of the respective zone authorised by the commander, and so on and so forth. Now, I'm interested in a particular sentence in the penultimate paragraph, which says: "Assistant chiefs shall -- are duty-bound, in addition to deploying the VP units in combat and their re-subordination to the commander of the HVO, to secure the permanent functional links between all the VP units," military police units, "as well as links to the Military Police Administration." So is it true and correct that units of the military police who, at a certain point in time, are subordinated to military commanders, whether of the operative zone or to the brigades, do they still remain functionally and administratively linked and within the composition of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, those who are deployed in combat are still functionally linked, they remain functionally linked. Well, they go about their regular military police duties, and they have their responsibilities towards the Military Police Administration, so everything remains the same in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll be talking about brigade platoons, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to follow up. I fail to understand. Military police units are re-subordinated for combat activities under the command of an HVO military commander. Are you saying that at the same time they are still charged with doing their normal police duties, or is it only that for administration, such as payment, certain logistical matters, perhaps, they remain with the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're talking about the light assault battalions placed under the command of the HVO, so all the other units in the operative zone carry out their regular military police duties; that is, controlling the check-points, going out on patrol, investigating crimes. And in administrative terms, they relied on the Military Police Administration and were linked to the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So there's a clear difference. Those that are engaged in combat, they are combat soldiers, full stop, and the others, they remain policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow on from my previous question, and we said this clearly earlier on. Judge Trechsel forgot to take that into account. The light assault battalions re-subordinated for combat assignments, that's what we were talking about. They're not permanently under the control of the army, if I can put it that way, but they are re-subordinated for a certain area, for a certain task, for a certain period of time. That is what we can deduce from the answers you've given us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Counsel, they are being re-subordinated. They were re-subordinated to carry out tasks issued to them by an HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And everything else that you stated is as you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another follow-up question. I listened to the questions that were put to you, as well as to your answers, and I looked at the documents. For those who know how it works, there is no problem to understand this. But for those who don't know, there might be some issues there. If I understand correctly, the military police has three main tasks: assault battalions, so they are combat units; second task, they do check-points on roads; and third task, they carry out investigations when crimes are committed. So if I understand correctly what you've just said, as for combat operations, they are under the authorities of the OZ commander. As for the other two tasks that they carry out, namely, manning the check-points as well as investigations, they have a link, a functional link, with the Military Police Administration. Is that how we should understand the way the military police operates on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the active-duty battalion, in addition to the light assault battalion, carried out normal military police tasks, unless certain companies or platoons were engaged in combat. As far as check-points are concerned and crime investigation, they were also under the command then of the commander of the operative zone, and they were functionally linked to the administration. If a convoy -- a military convoy were to appear, or military unit, or ammunition, or that kind of thing, then they would have to be given instructions from the military police saying that somebody would arrive at a check-point. So those are the things that they would have to deal with. But that relates to check-points. Otherwise, it was the commander of the operative zone who issued orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hadn't quite -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, for interrupting, but the witness is speaking very quickly, so some of what he said was left out of the transcript. Could he repeat the final part of what he said, but slowly, linked to what he said to crime investigation, on-scene crime investigation? Could he repeat that, because not everything was recorded. And when he was talking about informing the Military Police Administration, if a military convoy turns up, and that he received from the military police instructions about check-points, he did explain this, but it wasn't properly recorded because he was speaking extremely quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, could you please repeat slowly what you said, because what you're saying is very important, and if some sentences are missing, then there is a serious risk that Judges will make mistakes when they assess what you've just said when doing their deliberations, which, of course, as you know, are secret. So please repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me repeat. In the North-West Herzegovina OZ, in addition to the assault battalions, there was also an active-service battalion which performed regular police duties unless parts of the -- its platoons and companies were directly deployed in combat. As far as the work at check-points was concerned, as well as investigations, we were also subordinated to the commander of the OZ, who gave us tasks and orders. As far as our relationship with the MP Administration, we reported to them if there were some events at check-points, also if crimes were committed in the area of responsibility, and we did that through our daily and weekly reports sent to them. However, all the tasks were carried out and finished in the North-West Herzegovina OZ with the command thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. I'm still not quite clear as to what happens in the case of crime investigations. I will give you a case study. A crime is committed somewhere in the operational command zone. From that point in time, is that the commander of the OZ who will ask you to launch an investigation? But if this commander asks you to do nothing, will you do nothing? Or regardless of the instructions you may receive from this commander, will you, of your own accord, launch your own investigation? Do you understand what I mean? Did you understand my question? So what are you answering to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if a crime was committed and if the OZ commander was not informed or if nobody of his associates were informed, on the assumption that we were the ones who heard about that crime -- for example, if I heard about that crime, then I would send the MP and the Crime Investigation Department to the site to carry out an on-site inspection, but I will also inform the commander of the OZ or the commander who was in that zone of responsibility at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll use another case. The commander of the OZ has known of a crime being committed. You're also aware that a crime was committed. But what I'm wondering is whether the commander of the OZ can tell you not to launch any investigation, and in this case you will abide by this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it never happened. Therefore, I really don't know what to answer. I know that the OZ commander where I worked, if he heard about a crime, he made sure that the police did their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's just add something to the last question put to you by His Honour Judge Antonetti, or, rather, let me help you with it. The question was hypothetical, and you said it never happened. Bearing in mind the terminology in the police proceedings -- in the crime investigation proceedings that is used in our parts, I would put Judge Antonetti's last question in the following way: The military police, and men in the military police, did they prosecute and investigate crimes ex officio or because somebody told them to do so? And then if you answer that, everything will become clear. So if a person -- a member of the military police learns about a crime that was committed, did -- will that person go to that place on his own -- on his own initiative, or would such a person wait for somebody from the police -- Military Police Administration, or whoever tell them to go there and investigate the crime? I would like to hear your answer to that.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a good question, Counsel. The military police are duty-bound ex officio to investigate crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that everything is clear now. And the question put to you before that by the honourable Judge is a question that you also didn't answer fully. Let's try and clarify. We were talking about the functional and operational links, and let's be very specific and talk about the battalion under your command. At the moment or during the time while you were subordinated to an OZ and performing certain tasks, who was the one who was giving you operative military commands and orders?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it would be the commander of the OZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the same time, as we have just read in Mr. Coric's letter, at that same time, you had functional and administrative links with your own superior, as it were, and through those links you performed all your tasks and you had all your other needs met; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So let's summarise what you have just said. Irrespective of the nature of your tasks, be it military tasks or military policing tasks, your functional links were always to your police administration, and the operative links could be the links of the military police or the links of the OZ in this particular case; would that be correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that we have exhausted this matter and that we have managed to clarify it completely. I would kindly ask you to look at the following document, which is 3D03813. We started talking about different forms of activities of the military police, and then we focused on assault battalions. I believe that this document suggests, and you can confirm whether it's true or not, this is an order signed by you personally at the beginning of 1994; you reacted to an order issued by Siljeg who at that moment was a member of the MP Administration, no longer in the OZ, and here you send the 15 members of the 2nd Company to Uskoplje. You give them a very precise deployment, and you say that one day they will be on the line, one day they will act as police officers, one day they will act as an intervention group; again, policemen, in other words. And it says that your men should be subordinated to the commander, and so on and so forth. Do we agree that this group of yours, in case this order was carried out, that that's the way it changed its hats? One day, its hat said, I'm a soldier and I'm on the line. The second day, on its hat it says, I'm a military policeman and I'm in charge of order and -- peace and order in the village. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, first of all, you said that I signed this order. I didn't. This is not my signature. Second of all, this order was based by the chief of the Military Police Administration. The way we were issued the order, that's how we acted, literally. The chief of the MP Administration, Mr. Siljeg, issued this order, and we followed that order word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you denying the veracity of this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the document we have before us is problematic. Colonel Siljeg, who replaced Mr. Coric, is in charge of the military police, and he gives an order assigning military police officers in three different situations. One day, they're sent to combat; another day, they have to deal with military police issues; and then another day, they are part of an intervention group. Therefore, he decides how the policemen will be assigned to various tasks. In this order, I don't see that the Operational Zone commander has given his agreement. However, this could be of interest to him, because for him military policemen should be -- should spend two days on the front-line and not just one. However, reading this order, I recalled what I would do when I was in charge of the military police. I was commanding hundreds of military police officers who were in charge of carrying out regular military police tasks, and if I had been sent such an order, this would have caused a lot of problems for me, because I would have felt that I needed to be consulted first before military police officers were used for military tasks, because they were used before that for investigations. Now, this is what I would like to know: When Mr. Siljeg made that decision, he's, in fact, saying to the Operational Zone commander, This is what you have to do, without consulting him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as this order is concerned, as you can see, this order was sent to the Tomislavgrad Military District - you can see that under item 3 - which means that the commander of the Tomislavgrad Military District was informed about the dispatching of that company. And then in the body of the order, under item 3, it says men shall be subordinated to the platoon commander of the MP Uskoplje, and that person was subordinated to the brigade commander in Uskoplje when it came to the execution of his combat duties, which means that bullet point 2, item 1, where it says "one day on the line," that means that the MPs were sent to the line as given to him by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the very fact that the Tomislavgrad OZ commander was informed, was solving the problem, which means that if he didn't agree with that, he would let the other person know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, I'm being told that you have eight minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe two or three more questions would clarify the matter completely, but I don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the documents that you were provided with earlier today. We're talking about three separate documents. I apologise, hold on, hold on. I have something else to ask you before that. P1350, which was shown to you by my learned friend on Monday, P035 -- P01350, this is a record of the meeting held on the 29th of January in Ljubuski. I'm not sure that you said, when you talked about this document, that Mr. Praljak had called that meeting, or did you just say that he had attended that meeting? You obviously understand the difference between the two, between calling a meeting and attending it.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, as far as I remember, I said and I believe -- or, rather, I said that General Praljak had called that meeting, or at least that's what had been told to me. That's the information I had received in my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who told you that General Praljak had called the meeting? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I believe that it was the duty operations officer who called me, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Praljak or his secretary who called you to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not duty-bound to call me. The duty operation officer from the MP Administration called me to ask me to be -- to attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to your best recollection, what were you told? It was 15 years ago, of course.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Counsel, but it doesn't have to be the case, the duty operation officer of the MP Administration called me and told me that on that day there would be a meeting, and that that meeting was being organised by General Praljak, and that the MP Administration chief, Valentin Coric, would also attend that meeting after having returned from his hospital treatment. And he also told me to be accompanied by several officers from the MP battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It follows from the minutes - I believe that you will agree with me - that only General Praljak, who is listed first as attending, that he is the only one who is not a member of the MP or the MP Administration; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We also see further on in the minutes that the chief of the UVP, Mr. Valentin Coric, addressed the meeting and that his words were followed by General Praljak's words, that he had to answer some questions, and then we see, after a short break -- and so on and so forth. And my question is this: I'm putting it to you that Mr. Praljak was just a guest at that meeting. Bear that in mind when I put my following question to you. Would it be part of our culture -- would it be part of our meeting culture to have the host delivering the opening statement to a group of -- a meeting of some 40 people? Isn't that a social custom, that the host opens the meeting? Just say, Yes, or, No, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And, similarly, given our cultural practice, would the host then give the floor to the guest, the most important guest, if there are several guests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then after the guest's speech and after several questions have been put to the guest, there was a short break; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in the minutes. Have a look. After a short break, Z. Andabak, VP commander in action from the very beginning, and so on and so forth. So it's the first paragraph about the presence of guests. Then it says: "At the beginning of the meeting ..." Do you see where it is?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, but I don't remember a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember that later, during the course of that meeting -- regardless of whether you remember the break or not, do you remember having seen General Praljak again?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, General Praljak was still present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you claim that he was at the meeting all the time, to the best of your recollection, of course?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't understand that. Could you be more precise, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't know whether he was present until the very end, but I know that he spent quite a lot of time at the meeting. If you want me just to answer by saying, Yes, or, No, who the host was, and so on and so forth, well, I can say that I know why General Praljak was there. I came to learn about that in the course of the speeches given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you read the minutes, you can see that the discussion has to do about internal military police problems that have to do with organisation on the whole, problems that have to do with suppling people and so on and so forth. It has to do with the life and work of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is correct. I don't know what's in dispute here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I need you to confirm this for the sake of the transcript. You know, you're testifying, not me. And the minutes also show that General Praljak no longer participated in that discussion. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, General Praljak, as I can see in the minutes, no longer participated in the discussions, but General Praljak was very familiar with the field. And at this meeting, we discussed MP problems with regard to materiel and technical equipment, with regard to other sorts of equipment. And General Praljak was there, I believe, to hear about the problems we were facing. Well, in fact, he was very familiar with these problems because he had spent more time in the field than in the office. So he was very familiar with the situation in the field, so perhaps he was the competent person -- he was perhaps the right person to issue an order to someone in his HQ and tell them to assist us when trying to solve our problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I just want to check something with regard to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you've run out of time, so please wrap up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I could just have another two minutes to put another two questions to the witness and then to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- tell me, according to this document, Ljubica Jukic took these minutes. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not very well. I can't really remember who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know where she worked, for whom she worked?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, she worked in the MP Administration and worked in the field of supplies, logistics, for those who were wounded and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more time. I've distributed some documents, 3D03814, 15, and 16. Could I just ask the witness to confirm that these are the usual documents, documents that exist quite regularly? I don't have time to show him, but they show what sort of work the military police had to do, the typical kind of work they had to do. If the witness could just have a look at those documents and confirm that these are quite traditional documents, standard documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you know that you have a lot of difficulties in tendering documents. That's the least one can say. Those documents are not coming from the witness. He hasn't signed those documents, so I don't know -- I don't even know whether he's seen those documents. Those three documents may actually be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honours. That's why I would like to ask the witness whether he has perhaps seen these documents or, in the alternative, whether these are standard reports drafted by the military police platoon, the kind of reports that he has already referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, put the question to him, and the Trial Chamber will decide. I can't tell you anything at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Yes, of course, I'm not asking you to admit them into evidence in advance, but it might be a possibility if the witness does confirm these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I think there is an easier way to put it. You're just asking for some more minutes, because that's what it's about. You want to have the witness for a few more minutes, and the President will perhaps consult with us and we give you a few more minutes, because that's what it boils down to. We cannot -- we cannot use a document issue to bypass the time issue, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have five more minutes for the three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to insist on this so that I don't have to write lengthy opinions at a later stage. Please, please, emphasise the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yesterday -- on Monday, in fact, you spoke about platoons from the Military Police Brigade. At one point in time, you gave an almost complete description of their regular tasks, regular responsibilities. I wanted to ask you some other questions about that today, but I have no more time. We know what sort of responsibilities they had. And if you have been able to have a look at these three documents, if you've been able to have a look at what it's about, we don't need to go into the details. My question would be as follows: Do these three documents clearly demonstrate the regular duties -- the various regular duties that the brigade military police within the brigade had to perform? That's my first question, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we, the accused, haven't received these documents, I have no idea what we are dealing with. I would like to see these documents on screen so that we can follow what's going on in the courtroom. We have no idea because we haven't received these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for the sake of the transcript, the documents are 3D03814, and then 3815, 3816. The second one's up on the screen now -- the first one. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we're being shown these three documents, I have a sub-question for you. Do you know the person who signed here, the platoon commander, Ivan Kristo? He signed all three documents.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I can see, this is the Krajl Tomislav Brigade from Tomislavgrad, and commander Ivan Kristo was the commander of the brigade military police. So, yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now that you've had a look at the documents, tell me, all the tasks referred to, would you say that these are the typical tasks that a military police platoon has to carry out in the course of its regular work?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, from what I can see, they acted in accordance with an order from someone from the brigade who had been authorised by the commander to issue such orders. Perhaps in the last order, it says, When the military police contacts you, the Intervention Platoon of the Military Police went into a zone. So it was according to an order that certain military police tasks were carried out that weren't really tasks that were within their field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But when you look at the first document, 3814, when you look at the duties mentioned, it says, As ordered by the Defence Department, they went to inform Fejzic to report to the office. That's what you mentioned, bringing in soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is all within the domain of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And could we then just conclude, not to waste any more time. Did you see or would you agree that reports of this kind, with such subject matters, existed in the thousands, because each brigade platoon wrote such reports every day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the brigade military police submitted reports on a daily basis to its brigade commander on its work on a given day, so there were certainly reports on what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And would you say that the duties described in these three documents are regular duties, these regular reports?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yes. Yes, it says bring in soldiers, leave investigations, controls within the zone of responsibility, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Witness. Just a minute, please. Thank you, Your Honours. I have now concluded. I wanted to deal with the subject of the brigade police through several documents, but we'll do that on some other occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next Defence counsel. Ms. Alaburic, given the thick file that has been given to us, could you please remind us how much time you've been given?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd first like to greet you and everyone in the courtroom. Good day, Mr. Andabak. Thanks to your decision that you handed down, in which you granted us 20 additional minutes, we have a total of 32 minutes. I've tried to organise my cross-examination so that I can cover all subjects of importance. And if I fail to do so and you believe that my examination is relevant, I'd like you to -- I'd like to request a little more time. But I'll try and complete this in 32 minutes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't receive any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my colleague is providing them to me now. Thank you. We apologise for not reacting on time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andabak, I'm Vesna Alaburic, counsel from Zagreb. I represent General Petkovic, and I have a few questions on his behalf. If I have understood your biography, your curriculum, correctly, you were the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police from the 10th of February, 1993, until the end of December 1993; is that correct -- end of November 1993, correction, until the end of November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you were chief of the Department of the General Military Police, your work was in Mostar, is that correct, that's where your position was?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Mostar and in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mostar and Ljubuski aren't in the territory of the Operative Zone of North-Western Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you spoke about the term -- or used the term "zone of responsibility." You mentioned kilometres, depth, and breadth, that had to do with the zone of responsibility. 50943 is the page in the transcript I'm referring to. My question is as follows: What you said -- please listen to me, Mr. Andabak. The information you provided in your answer, is such information you obtained in some sort of handbook, information that was relayed to you, or information that you, yourself, invented?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the zone of responsibility and its breadth --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. Tell me, did you read about this, were you told about it, or did you invent this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, madam, what it was like on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you where you got the information from. Where did you get the information from about this in-depth distance of 15 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That piece of information I received from commanders on the ground, according to how they determined their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since you were a member of the military police, Witness, and not the army, I'm going to tell you that as far as the army is concerned, there's the zone of attack and the zone of defence, or area of attack and area of defence. Now, this 15 kilometres of yours, does it refer to the area of attack or the area of defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before he answers the question, I think counsel's testifying. Now, she can say that a witness came in here, she can point to a document, but as far as I know, she's not a witness, and she hasn't served in the military. So for her to be giving -- to be telling the witness what she thinks, you know, is correct, is totally improper. She can point at a document. Otherwise, I object. She's leading, and she's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Alaburic, Mr. Karnavas is correct, if one follows common-law rules. It is true that in your country and in mine, you could have asked such a question, but here the practice is such that it is better to proceed step by step. And here, in your question, you are stating that there could have been an attack in a zone of defence. Before you get there, please ask some preliminary question. Otherwise, you will be the one testifying and Mr. Karnavas will be fully right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to acknowledge that I wasn't following the translation of my question, so I can't say with any certainty whether it was properly interpreted. But what you've just said that I asked, that is not what I asked. That wasn't my question. I spoke about the zone of attack and zone of defence, which are military terms in all military manuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you don't know the answer, just say so and we can move on. So do you know what the concept and term "zone of attack" and "zone of defence" means?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what the "zone of attack" and "zone of defence" means now at this point in time, I can't really tell you, I can't give you a definition.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, Witness, in your proofing sessions for your testimony, did you decide with the Prlic Defence that you would be asked questions about the concept of "area of responsibility," that term?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, we haven't met, so there's no mystery about this. And, second of all, I do take offence, because now my character and my professionalism is being impugned. This may be appropriate in Zagreb. It is not appropriate anywhere else. She can do this when she's practicing the type of law that she does practice, which is not criminal defence law, but this is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. You are talking about proofing, but Mr. Karnavas says there hasn't been any proofing. So what's your take?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness can say that he never talked to Jadranko Prlic's Defence counsel and that he didn't make any agreement with them about this, and there's no problem there. I don't mind the witness giving that answer and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is an insinuation. There lies the problem. Now, if I were in court in the United States, I would call my colleague is engaging in sleazy tactics. That's what this is all about. It impugns the integrity of counsel, it calls into question his ethics and professionalism. It means that counsel is somehow conniving with the witness. That's the implication, and I object to it. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, since this is Mr. Coric's Defence witness, I have to join in what Mr. Karnavas has said and say that I'm offended too, personally, because this was a witness who attended a proofing session with the Coric Defence, and, therefore, the Coric Defence did not make any agreements with the witness with respect to what the witness was going to say in the Coric Defence case, let alone anything else, because we don't tell the witnesses what they're supposed to say. So we don't reach any agreements with witnesses, and let alone would we do this in the interests of another accused in the courtroom. And the witness can speak for himself, so that I don't have to speak in his stead, whether ever before coming into this courtroom he ever saw any of the Defence counsel of Mr. Jadranko Prlic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Everybody should slow down, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll certainly take Judge Prandler, whom I can barely see, but good morning, Judge Prandler, around this pillar. But I'll take that advice. But in an attempt to lower the temperature, and sitting here, knowing and working with Ms. Alaburic and, of course, knowing what it is she's trying to do, but also, like Mr. Karnavas, coming from a common-law jurisdiction, he is taking unnecessary offence there. There was, of course, an implicit, if you like, question in Ms. Alaburic's question as to whether, in the proofing sessions, plural, there was a proofing session with the Prlic counsel. That was easily answered. Either the witness did have such a proofing session or he didn't. But it's a fair assumption that he had proofing sessions generally, and there is an important distinction here. There was nothing in Ms. Alaburic's question which suggested any sort of collusion, any impropriety, in relation to what answers might be given. What was asked, if there was indeed a proofing session with the Prlic Defence - and if there wasn't, of course, and we're told there wasn't, I think, then that would be an end to the story - did they decide he would be asked questions about the concept? There is nothing at all wrong, in a proofing session, with discussing what questions will be asked. There is certainly something wrong with priming a witness as to what the answers might be, but heaven knows if you don't discuss with a witness, in a proofing session, what questions might be asked, then the question arises as to what you're doing having a proofing session at all. So there was absolutely nothing wrong whatsoever, and I can certainly speak for Ms. Alaburic and myself, as Mr. Petkovic's counsel, in saying there was not the slightest insinuation of unprofessionalism by Mr. Karnavas or anybody else in relation to this. And please, Mr. Karnavas, don't be so thin-skinned, I say through Your Honour, and jump to your feet so quickly and see such allegations made against you, because they are not made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Stewart, you're partly right and partly wrong. I agree that I did not see, in this question, an attack on Mr. Karnavas' professional/ethical standing, but the question is wrong in that it assumes a fact for which there is no basis. You assume that there was a briefing session with the Prlic Defence, and then on that basis, for which there is no foundation, you ask about the content, what happened during such a questioning. You ought to have asked first whether there was any proofing, and then you could have gone on. But to presume such a fact, that was not correct. So I think you should reformulate or go somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I just say the reformulation, of course, is for Ms. Alaburic, who's asking the questions. I'm extremely pleased to know that on the more important point on what I got to my feet for, I'm extremely pleased to know that Your Honour accepts what I've said. As far as the question, the formulation is concerned, I did acknowledge that there was implicit, in Ms. Alaburic's question, the issue or the question as to whether there was or wasn't a proofing session. So, Your Honour, I'm not -- on behalf of Ms. Alaburic and myself, I'm not going to squabble with either part of what Your Honour has just said, respectfully, but I am very pleased to know that Your Honour, like me, saw nothing by way of insinuation of unprofessionalism by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your understanding. I personally don't feel the need to response to what Mr. Karnavas said. And apart from that, Mr. Stewart has said it all. Perhaps I asked a rather unwieldy question, but what I was asking was whether the witness had been to a proofing session, because we knew that he came in on Thursday and it was quite normal that a witness attends proofing sessions, just as all our witnesses did. So I thought my question was proper. I wanted to know whether, within the frameworks of that proofing, they had any conversations with a previous Defence, and I mentioned Mr. Prlic. But as I say, I don't feel the need to belabour the point or ask any further questions about that. I was just interested in how you came by that piece of information and whether you happened to read about it in some manual. But with your permission, Your Honours, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Andabak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness raises his hand. I believe he has something to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With your permission, I'd like to say the following. I'd just like to respond to the counsel. As far as the area of responsibility is concerned, books are one thing, the terrain and the situation on the ground is another. So I'm telling her what my experience was on the ground because that's where I performed my duties, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I thought that you might have referred to a manual, which is known in the courtroom as the rules governing brigades, Rules on Brigades, so I thought that you might have read about that there. But I'll move on. Witness, do you happen to know that the new leadership of the Ministry of Defence, at the end of 1993, gave a negative assessment to the work of the military police from its inception until that period, that is to say, December 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I don't know about that, and I don't know what new leadership in the Ministry of Defence you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The first document that you have in your binder is document P7169, and it is the minutes from a meeting of the military police officers held on the 14th of December, 1993. And at that meeting, you were in attendance, and -- or Mr. Lavric said at the meeting that the assessment and evaluations of the work of the military police were not satisfactory. Listen to me carefully, Mr. Andabak. They were not satisfactory, and this would require a re-establishment of the military police. And according to these minutes, on page 7 of the Croatian text, it says that you, Mr. Andabak, wanted to know who gave you this negative mark for your work up until then. And Colonel Biskic responded by saying that the military police was given negative assessments and appraisals for its work as a whole, but that your 2nd Light Assault Battalion was given a high mark, a high assessment, by Mr. Biskic personally. So do you remember now this assessment and appraisal of the work of the military police in those terms?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I'll be happy to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether you remember that or not. Do you recall it or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, allow me to answer. You asked me, so I'm going to answer. What I remember is this --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just interested in whether you recall this, because I don't have time to allow you to go into details, but you will have time if the Judges want to hear about it and give me more time.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there's something that's not been correctly observed and concluded here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in whether you remember those negative appraisals.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if I need to go into details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with your questions and with your answers. I don't know why you do not understand this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On another point: Witness, you are in the disagreeable -- not enviable situation of being cross-examined, and almost every witness must be told about the special rules that apply in this. And the basic rule is that the counsel carrying out cross-examination leads you and has the right to put questions that need a short answer, Yes, No, I don't know, I don't remember. There may be exceptions, but generally you are -- and you may regret this, and we understand that you may regret this, but you do not have the right to explain everything you would like to explain. So Ms. Alaburic must be supported in this, and she can ask you just to limit your answer. And I will invite to you comply with this, because it's in the Rules and it is necessary to contain the time needed. Please, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, Witness, at the end of 1993, were the brigade platoons of the military police abolished?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I can't remember when they were abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that they were abolished at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were abolished, and I think there was a new establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, were they abolished because they weren't functional?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that with the re-establishment, the guards brigades were set up, so there was no need for them to exist anymore within the frameworks of the municipal brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that they were functioning or were not functioning properly? The brigade military police platoons, were they functioning well or not, and were they abolished because they were working and functioning well or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I can't really tell you, because I wasn't in the brigade military police, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a suggestion to make to be of assistance in these proceedings, to ensure that they run smoothly. Counsel is asking general questions, just like the last one there, whether the brigade police platoons functioned properly or not, yes or no. Can you imagine how many military platoons there were in existence, and now this man here, who's a professional and a military commander from the war, a practitioner, he's being asked to give a yes-or-no answer, some were, some weren't, perhaps I'm speaking on the assumption. But to make a general sweeping statement and conclusion, only nonprofessionals can do that, not professionals. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no need to respond to that. But I was just quoting Mr. Marjan Biskic, and we had occasion to hear him here as a leading military expert in the military police in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, my next question is this: During the examination-in-chief, you were shown document P990, which is the next document in your binder. It's an order from the brigade commander to relieve of duty the commander of the brigade military police, Ante Prlic, and your answer was that that was in keeping with the remit and authorisations of the brigade commander and that you knew that the Military Police Administration did not appoint commanders of brigade platoons of the military police. I'm now going to put to you the testimony of a protected witness here, so for that may we move into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness, according to your experience with the military police, was such a situation possible?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, I was in the OZ for a long time, and I was also in South-East Herzegovina, and I can tell you that this is not normal. The brigade commander had all the authorities, and nobody from the administration could interfere with his authorities to hire and dismiss people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the following document, which is 4D2041. This is a document from the military police which refers to the dismissal of the commander of the brigade military police in Citluk. And here the military police say -- or, rather, Andrija Buhovac on behalf of the military police, it says that the brigade commander does not have the competence to hire and fire the commander of the brigade police, that the brigade commander can only request from the MP Administration to remove the commander of the brigade police from his duties. Mr. Andabak, according to what you know, such an answer which came from the military police, is this answer legal or illegal? Is it lawful or unlawful?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this piece of paper is somebody's improvisation, and if you can -- will allow me, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you whether this is lawful or unlawful.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a forgery. Somebody abused the letterheaded paper of the MP Administration. I know that this is not an original. Mr. Santic was removed under the request of the brigade commander, and if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm only interested in the answer.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have Andrija Buhovac here. This is not his signature. This isn't the signature of General Jelic. Somebody forged this signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, do you see here that somebody signed this on behalf of that person, just like the document which contains your name and somebody signed on your behalf? Is that a rule, that somebody can sign on somebody's behalf?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know, madam. I don't know that the commander of the defence of the city of Mostar would sign on behalf of a company commander. There is no logic in that. If you look at this, you can see that number 3 was added to -- next to the name of the Military Police Administration chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were you stating that this document is a forgery; is that what you're saying, is that your testimony? Can you please speed up.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation, madam. Madam, somebody actually abused the letterheaded paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it's a forgery?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, towards the end of 1993, in addition to the brigade platoons of the military police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I just want to draw your attention to the fact that we have no translation of the relevant document here. We have it in Croatian, and we are all a bit poor in our Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what could be the reason. It is in e-court. There is no reason for you not to have the translation. The translation has been translated and was already used during General Petkovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I found it. I'm sorry. It was hidden from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Colonel, I listened to what you say. You said it was a forged document. So what would have been the interest of creating this false document? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this document from the MP Administration, Ivan Santic may have gotten a hold of the letterheaded paper himself. We lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and during the wartime there are not so many typewriters, and one could get hold of any stamp. You just had to have 15 German marks to buy it, which means that the company commander did not even have to have the letterheaded paper of the MP Administration. I didn't have to have it, as the battalion commander. I could put any heading I wanted, the OZ, the 2nd Battalion, the location where I was deployed, anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understood. You're saying that Andrija Buhovac, the one who is signing as the commander of the 4th Company of the 5th VP Battalion, this person could not have signed because he could not have had this document with a letterhead "Military Police Administration," this was impossible; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct. The document, itself, when you look at it, you can see that Andrija Buhovac didn't sign it, that on his behalf it was signed by the commander of the defence of the city of Mostar. There is no logic to that. How could I, for example, have signed on behalf of a company commander in my own battalion? Which means that somebody played games with this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, therefore, the number 024/30400/93 is actually a false number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the number is 02-4/1, but then it was made to look like a "3." This is a paper from the MP Administration, which would mean that the MP Administration sent a document to itself, and there is no logic to that. And that's why I'm saying that this is not an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This apart, Witness, in substance, is what is written here correct? Is it correct to say that the brigade commander is not competent to dismiss an officer of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the biggest idiocy on the paper. The brigade commander is the one who hires and fires the commander of the brigade military police, and the administration have nothing whatsoever to do with that. And I say this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: How is this compatible with the other information you gave us; namely, that as far as the functional situation is concerned, the military police stays under the authority of the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's still a link, but it is well known what the MP Administration did. They were in charge of hiring and firing commanders. It did not have any authority over the brigade platoons of the military police, but it was responsible for providing logistics by means of sending them uniforms, insignia, and providing professional training of the brigade MPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you said this document was signed by the commander of the defence of the city of Mostar. Could you please tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, the commander of the defence of the city of Mostar was Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that Zlatan Mijo Jelic signed this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I'm sure that somebody abused Zlatan Mijo Jelic's signature and that this signature is a forgery. His signature was very simple to forge, to falsify. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Hold on, hold on. I apologise. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Just a technical issue, please. The witness should be shown the stamp, the big stamp. This is the stamp of the MP Administration, which means that it was made and it was recorded twice in the MP Administration. One has to ask him whether this is an MP stamp and what he knows about signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, the incoming stamp, could you please tell us whose incoming stamp this is?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it's not very legible, so I wouldn't be able to tell you. I can see that the number does belong to the MP Administration, and I've already told you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that number on the incoming stamp, would that also be a number of the MP Administration?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It should be checked. In any case, it starts with a "3," and it should be, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In August 1993, what was Zlatan Mijo Jelic's function in the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, during that period of time, Zlatan Mijo Jelic was a member of the MP, but he did not have anything to do with the MP because he commanded the defence of the city of Mostar. He was the commander of the defence of the city of Mostar, so he could not use the MP stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that he did not have any function in the military police; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I am saying that he was the commander of the city of Mostar defence and that he did not have any other duties in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that we have reached the time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take a break. The Registrar has informed me that you have 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the meantime, during the break, we have distributed a document. P3487 is its number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, just one question. The document in question is a decision issued by Mr. Bruno Stojic on the 16th of July, 1993. And in that decision it says that Zlatan Mijo Jevic was appointed as the assistant chief of the MP Administration for the South-East Herzegovina OZ. My question is this: Did you know that Mr. Jelic had the function similar to the one that you had for the North-West Herzegovina OZ or the same as you had there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't know whether it was Zlatan Mijo Jevic or Zeljko Dzidic who was the assistant chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, a few words about light assault battalions of the military police. Tell us, were they abolished towards the end of 1993? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, light assault brigades --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Battalions.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- battalions of the military police were abolished as a result of the new establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When it comes to those light assault battalions of the MP, did they become the guards brigades of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, some of the staff of the light assault battalions did make the base of the newly-established brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, according to the regulations that were in effect in Herceg-Bosna, who was authorised to issue orders to light assault battalions of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my OZ, it was the OZ commander, and that was the case elsewhere as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In document P975 [sic], which is the next document in your binder, you will see that the document was co-signed by Mr. Coric and Stojic about the organisation of the military police. And it says that the 1st Battalion is active duty and directly linked to the Military Police Administration, and that upon the chief's orders it may be deployed across the entire area of Herceg-Bosna. The 1st Company is a light assault unit. Tell us, please, from what I have just read to you, what can you tell us? Who has the right to issue orders to a light assault unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, we are talking about the organisation which was in effect in December 1992, so I'm expecting a different question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, from what we have just read, who had the right to issue orders to a light assault unit when it was not re-subordinated? The basic rule, who was in command? Could you please give us the name?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The light assault company is subordinated to the commander of the 1st Active-Duty Battalion, and it is the Administration of the Military Police who issues orders to the 1st Light-Duty Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct the number of the document. It should be P957.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, did you read the book "Three Years of Military Police," which is P586 -- 8548 in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't read the book, but I did see a copy when I came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll just refer to one sentence from an article written by Radoslav Lavric, and it says that light assault battalions gradually developed into purely military units. Would you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us, in 1993 was Mr. Lavric also the deputy chief of the military police and then, for a certain period of time, an acting chief of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I can't remember what his position was in 1993. I know that he was the deputy chief for a certain period of time, but as to what he was later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, what was the main purpose -- the main function of these light assault units? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, as far as the light assault platoons -- battalions of the MP are concerned, they worked in their own operative zones and they were intended to carry out combat tasks in those zones where the commander of the OZ thought that they should be deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it means that their function was to engage in combat tasks, if I have understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, combat tasks. But they would also perform other military police duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Andabak, now have a look at a document that you have already seen on a number of occasions in this courtroom, P3778. This is an order from Valentin Coric, dated the 28th of July, 1993, on the re-subordination to the light assault platoons and to the HVO commander. In the introduction, Valentin Coric refers to an order from the head of the Defence Department. Mr. Andabak, do you know the reason for which Valentin Coric referred to Bruno Stojic's order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, as far as I can remember, so that the HVO commander wouldn't have such a distance when it came to moving units of the military police from one unit -- from one area to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's why Mr. Coric referred to Stojic's order, not to, for example, someone else's order in Herceg-Bosna. Do you know what the responsibilities were of the head of the Defence Department or, rather, of the minister of defence, when it comes to the re-subordination of MP units?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the responsibilities were of the minister of defence in respect of re-subordinating the MP to a certain military commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the minister of defence had no such authority to send someone in or to assign responsibility to someone to carry out certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, perhaps at this point I can alert my friend, for hopefully her assistance, that care be exercised in intermingling a comment with questions. It doesn't really assist.
