If one looks, for example, at page 46, line 18 and 19, we see a comment from counsel, followed by a question, and I think at this stage, in areas that perhaps are not so controversial as yet, if my learned friend can endeavour simply to put clear-cut questions and don't put comments to the witness. I think it would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask questions, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is clear. It consists of two sentences. There are no claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As there is an interruption, anyway: Witness, you have given an answer that I simply did not understand. You referred to -- you said why Mr. Coric referred to Mr. Stojic in that order that we have seen several times, and your answer is, I quote: "... so that the HVO commander wouldn't have such a distance when it came to moving units of the military police from one unit -- from one area to another." I must confess I do not understand what you mean by this sentence, so perhaps you could explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the 2nd Light Assault Battalion of the MP went to carry out a task in the operative zone in South-Eastern Herzegovina, in that case the commander of the operative zone would write a request to the Main Staff, and the Main Staff would deliver the request to the MP Administration, a request on engaging those units, and the unit would receive an order from the MP Administration for their engagement. So to have a briefer procedure, in terms of the bureaucratic procedure, the commander of the HVO could issue an order on his own without following the procedure according to which a unit should move from one zone to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And was Mr. Stojic a commander in that sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic wasn't a commander, because he was the minister of defence, but this order is based on an order of his which he forwarded to the MP Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I fail to understand why the minister of justice [sic], of whom we have often heard that he had no operative functions, he would not engage troops here and there, that now he takes the decision to send troops to a -- MP troops to a certain area or unit. As far as I seem to have understood the system, this is something which should come from the military command, being the General Staff or maybe Mr. Boban even. But would the minister of defence be competent to take such a decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the minister of defence wasn't competent. At one point in time, there was the position of an HVO commander that appeared, in the operative sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would then the answer to the question counsel put to you actually be that Mr. Coric refers to an order of Mr. Stojic, who, in turn, probably gave such order because there was a request by a military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know who made a request to whom, Your Honours. But in accordance with the order, as it says, from head of the department, the Defence Department, and on the basis of that order, the chief of the MP Administration drafted the order that he drafted. So in the field, there was an HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I cannot help but noticing that there is some fog in this area. This is really not quite clear, why Mr. Coric would refer to an order by Mr. Stojic to re-subordinate military police to a commander. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, now I will show you a series of documents about the authorities of the chief of the military police when it comes to commanding and ordering military police units, after which I will put a question to you. All the parts of the documents that I will refer to are in 4D2056. They can be found in that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, in the second group of documents you have the integral versions of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, it's sufficient for you to listen to me. The first document, P143, temporary instructions for the work of MP units, the date is April 1992, and it says that: "The MP Administration shall be organised within the HVO, and it shall control and command all military police units belonging to operative groups, organisational units, and the Military Police Administration." The following document, P837, instructions for the work of MP units, dated November 1992, it also says that: "The Military Police Administration shall command and order all MP units." P957, which we had a look at a minute ago, signed by Stojic and Coric on the 26th of December, 1992, and towards the end of the document it says that: "The MP Administration shall command and issue orders to all military police units." The following document, P956, a report from the MP -- the military police for 1992, and it says certain operative group commands have been established and they have been placed under a single command of the Military Police Administration. And then P5978 [as interpreted], it's a rule book on staffing and duties in the Military Police Administration. As chief of the Military Police Administration -- or: "The chief will issue orders to the military police units, to battalions in operative zones, and to the light assault brigade." That's in brackets. I'll repeat the document number, P978, 978. The following, P1635, a report from Valentin Coric to Mate Boban, dated the 9th of March, 1993. And it says: "The command structure is headed by the Military Police Administration, and the units are organised in the form of one brigade consisting of five battalions." The following document, P4300, Valentin Coric's order dated the 19th of August, 1993, states the following: It says that: "The brigade military police are, by order of the day, under the direct command of the brigade commander. The remaining platoons of general and traffic military police are under the command of the company commander who is responsible to the OZ battalion command. The chief of the MP Administration shall engage light assault units at the request of the assistant chief for the OZ." And the last document, P8309, rules on the work and organisation of the military police, issued in 1996, and the provisions are the same: "All MP units are subordinated to the MO Military Police Administration under the command and control of the head of the MO Military Police Administration." My question, Mr. Andabak, is as follows: Did you know that the rules of Herceg-Bosna dealt with the manner in which military police units were to be organised and led in this way? Mr. Andabak, did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam, what you have said, well, that's contained in the rules for the military police. You spoke about the rules for the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, is that the reason for which, on page 5094, you said that Mr. Coric was the main -- or the key person or top man in the military police? That's how it was translated into English. That's what you said about Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To your statement that Mr. Coric was the top man.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that statement of mine?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I gave you the page reference in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, as far as I remember, I certainly didn't say he was the top man. I said he was the chief of the administration and that he was in charge of the administration. That was the position that he held.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just provide you with the reference to the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait. Mr. Coric is on his feet. Would you like to say something, Mr. Coric? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I want to say two things. I have stood up, well, because the counsel showed documents about the organisation of military police units for various periods of time. That's good, but she also read out just a few sentences about my duties, in a general sense. Well, this isn't a statement now. I'm not someone from the HVO who would like to dismiss the military police. I'm proud of what I did in the war, of my role in the war, so I'm not washing my hands of this. But if the witness is examined in this way, I would request that in the future this examination follow a different procedure, because if the Croatian Army, for example, is now active in Afghanistan, does that mean that the command of the Croatian Army in Croatia is responsible for what they do there? I'm not dismissing or rejecting a single military police officer. I am proud of their good deeds, although there were certain misdeeds that were committed, but I know that on the whole the vast majority of these men were honourable men. Unfortunately, I couldn't issue orders to them as was sometimes necessary. In fact, I shouldn't even have issued orders or had command over the entire structure, but rather over just a small part. But 90 per cent of the tasks carried out by the military police were tasks for which others issued orders. Compare this to the situation in Afghanistan and to other operations in the world. This is quite normal. If anyone knows about how armies function, this is quite a normal situation. Thank you very much. This was a statement. I do apologise, but I wanted to assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, this is a statement, a statement that you can make when you will be testifying to assist the Chamber. Fine, it's been recorded in the transcript. Ms. Alaburic, the Registrar has informed me that you've run out of time. So you're asking for extra time now?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you saw, in the binder that I prepared, that I have three very short areas to deal with. And if you would give me a quarter of an hour to be deducted from the Petkovic Defence time, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated and think that there should be an equitable amount of time given to all the Defence counsel. The Praljak Defence was given seven extra minutes. You'll be allotted seven extra minutes, too, so please try to wrap up in seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you told us that -- and you were talking about the disarmament and isolation of Muslims in Livno - and on transcript page 50977 - that, at any rate, the active-duty military police had nothing to do with the detained Muslims. Do you remember that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the penultimate document in the binder. It's P3716, which is a report which Mr. Branimir Tucak, on the 26th of July, 1993 -- let me repeat the document number, P3716. Yes, 3716. 3716 is the document number. So Branimir Tucak is sending this report to Mr. Coric, and the subject is "The Action to Disarm the Livno Muslims." And it says that in that action, military police units participated, and that the 2nd Light Assault Battalion and the 3rd Company of the 6th Battalion of the Military Police. Now, my question to you is this: The units -- the MP units mentioned, were they within the category of the active-duty ones or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, these units were active battalions, and when you said that I had said that they hadn't taken part, what I'm saying is they didn't take part in the security of the locations they were in. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now look at the next document, P2202. This is an interim report which you, Mr. Andabak, judging by the document, are sending to Mate Boban, Bruno Stojic, and Valentin Coric, on the 5th of May, 1993. Let me repeat the document number, P2202. Tell us, Mr. Andabak, is this one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, yes, that is my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what it says in paragraph 3 from the bottom, where you say: "Relations between the Livno staff and the military police is bad, and the basic reason for that is that when the police needs something, and that the staff can solve, the response we're given is to contact Grude, Ljubuski, or Mostar for what we need, because," and in inverted commas, "'we were Boban's police,' said Ante Colak and others," and, once again in inverted commas, "'who sends you into the field. You are crazy.'" Tell us, Mr. Andabak, was the opinion about you in Livno that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that wasn't the prevailing opinion about us. This was the opinion of the local patriots. And that's how this letter came to be written in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Andabak -- we saw from the documents so far - and you were asked this during the examination-in-chief - that the MP unit that you were in command of was in combat in Gornji Vakuf in the course of January 1993. Now, my question: In the village of Uzricje and Zdrimci, did members of the military police enter those two villages? Let me repeat the name of the second village, Zdrimci, S-d-r-i-m-c-i [as interpreted], Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, January, the military police was predominantly located in the town itself, in Gornji Vakuf itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, in the report on the work of the military police, which is document P3090, on page -- listen to me. There's no need for you to waste time searching for the document. On page 6, the end of page 6 of the English, and the beginning of page 7 of the English, it says that members of the 2nd MP Battalion from Livno and Posusje had taken control of the village of Uzricje and also the village of Zdrimci, and that the units of the military police were commanded by the commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion and the commander of the 2nd MP Battalion. Now, my question is this: Is this report correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now look at document P610. You'll find it in the second part of the binder, or look at your screen. It will appear on e-court. It is Valentin Coric, a daily report for the 21st of October, 1992. And in the introduction, it says that: "Due to the events in Central Bosnia and pursuant to an order from the head of the Defence Department, we have sent a reinforcement from the 2nd Battalion." Now, my question to you, Mr. Andabak, is this: Do we have reason -- any reason not to believe that Mr. Coric compiled a true and correct report, a truthful report?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, this is good. The 2nd Battalion had already been given its assignment to Jajce with a company added.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether we have any reason to doubt Mr. Coric -- the truth of Mr. Coric's report.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he knows what he's on about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. And now the last document, because I think my time is almost up, P3889, which is your report, Mr. Andabak, about the departure of the military police from Livno to the location. On page 4 of the Croatian version, which is page 6 of the English, it says as follows: "The whole time on the ground in Gornji Vakuf --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat her question, because there's a lot of interference and noise in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat my question, yes. I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of the Croatian text and page 6 of the English text, it says as follows: "Throughout the time on the ground in Gornji Vakuf, Mr. Rade Lavric can give a report, who was also in several places where the military police of Livno was located, too, as well as members of the brigade, the Petar Kresimir IV Brigade." And my question to you is this: What function, in January 1993, did Rade Lavric occupy?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, Rade Lavric was the deputy chief of the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my last question: At the end of page 4, you speak about departures to Mostar, and you say that: "In the fighting in Mostar, members of the military police from Livno spent 18 days, so that four times more, pursuant to orders from Bruno Stojic, they went to Mostar and took part in the fighting against the Muslims there and rounding up deserters from the HVO of Mostar." Now, is that part of your report truthful or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you for allowing me additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to ask the Pusic Defence if they have any questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What about Mr. Prlic's Defence? Mr. Karnavas, do you have any questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, sir. We have no questions for the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So all the questions have been put by the various Defence teams. I have one last question to put to you, Mr. Witness. During your tenure as the commander of the 2nd Battalion, in all, how many casualties have you recorded there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't give you an exact figure, I can't remember, but there were quite a lot of men killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can you not give us a ballpark figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps between 40 and 50 killed, and maybe three times as many, if not more, wounded, seriously, less seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said between 40 and 50. Out of about 500 military men, military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So one could say that you had about 10 per cent of your men who were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's say, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to know. So, Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor for your own cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Andabak. Colonel, you're going to get a binder of documents, and in the next few hours we will discuss the documents in that binder. And to start off with, I want to show you a document that Mr. -- the counsel for Petkovic also showed you, which is P08548. You can find it in the binder. It's the publication entitled "Three Years of Military Police."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Bos. In order for your cross-examination to be carried out as best as possible, I would like to remind Colonel Andabak that you are in a phase of cross-examination. My colleague has mentioned it before, but it was dealing with counsel, so for the various Defence teams. But now you are in another phase where the Prosecutor is going to ask you questions. The Prosecutor is mastering his own time, which means that it will be up to him to decide which questions he's going to put to you. And, generally speaking, given that those Prosecutors have a common-law background, what they would like you to do is to answer by, Yes, No, or I don't know. And depending on your answer, they will move on or they will want to ask follow-up questions. The questions may not be of your liking, but this is the rule of the game. So please listen carefully to the question and answer according to the way the question was put to you. This is how it works here. Mr. Bos, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, Colonel Andabak, if I could ask you to look at Exhibit P08548, and this is a publication entitled "Three Years of Military Police," and it was also briefly shown to you by counsel for Petkovic. And I think you just said a moment ago that you had seen this document when you arrived here in The Hague. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And isn't this a publication where various prominent members of the HVO and -- in 1995 were asked to submit a contribution to this booklet, and that you, as well as Mr. Valentin Coric, made a contribution to this booklet?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, that is right. And it was published in 1995, but we were no longer members of the military police. We just gave our comments as far as its work was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, in this binder, we have the contributions made by Mr. Coric and by yourself, and I would like you first to look at the contribution made by Mr. Coric, which is on page 17 of the B/C/S version and page 23 of the English translation. And let me just read out a part from this contribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, my learned friend, but on page 61 -- oh, yes, it's been corrected, but it said that it was Mr. Stojic. But that was corrected, because there's no Mr. Stojic mentioned in the document. So that's all I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, let me read out a paragraph from the contribution made by Mr. Coric, and it's sort of the fifth paragraph of the document. It's on the middle column on the B/C/S version, right under the photograph. Let me read this out: "When selecting members of the military police, we took care to recruit honourable people, people committed to the Croatian cause and the homeland, and I think that we were very successful in that selection. Many of them proved themselves already in the first month, and some later during the war, and became prominent commanders of military and police units." Sir, you being a prominent member of the MP, were you also committed to the Croatian cause and the homeland?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you explain to the Court what it means to you when -- to be committed to the Croatian cause and the homeland, could you explain that to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that means that we aspire towards the survival of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because at the beginning of the war against the JNA, and with the Serb forces, that was what we aspired to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what does it mean when you refer to the homeland? Are we talking here about a territory?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The state Bosnia-Herzegovina; okay. Well, let me -- let's move on, and let's see what -- look at your contribution, which is on page 47 of the B/C/S version. It's the next document. It's page 72 of the English version. Let me just read out what -- a few of the things that you say, starting from the start -- from the top: "The war was already raging in these areas when I was assigned the command of the 2nd Military Police Battalion in Livno. I still remember with pride the songs [sic] of Croatia, without exception, voluntary joined the light assault battalion." And then skipping a few lines to the third paragraph: "And that is history written by members of this formation, in their own blood, on every --" MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. In the original text, there's no mention of songs about Croatia. Perhaps it would be a good idea if I were to -- well, I haven't received the English translation of the text, but perhaps the witness could read it out and it's the -- in the Croatian version, because there's nothing about these songs in the Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's not read "songs," it's read "sums," so I hope that will clarify the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's just continue on paragraph 3, what you say: "And what is history written by members of these formations, in their own blood, on every foot of Herceg-Bosna, everywhere where the homeland called." Now, sir, isn't it correct that Herceg-Bosna was part of the homeland and that the homeland you've been referring to here is the Croatian Banovina with the borders of the 1993 -- of the 1939 borders?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not talking about the Banovina here, but in 1993 there was the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna with a Croatian population. And as far as I know, we never wrote -- if you mean the homeland, the Republic of Croatia, we always had as our heading and title: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," "The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna" under that in all the headings and titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on to another topic. And for this, I think we need to go into private session, Your Honours, because I'd like to show the witness an exhibit which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's all the way in the back, Colonel, 5D04218.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a judgement from the Military Court in Livno, dated the 25th of November, 1994, so about a year later. And we see here a judgement, and we are -- in which three persons are being convicted for the crime of armed robbery, and two of the names, numbers 2 and 3, are, in fact, the two persons that we also saw in the first document. But what I'd like to point out is that if you read their backgrounds, it says -- well, I won't mention the name because I don't know whether that may be protected, but it says that neither of the two had any previous convictions. Sir, can we conclude from this that when these people were taken in in January for the crime of rape against Muslim women, that these people had not been prosecuted for that crime?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I didn't get involved in the work of the crime prevention police. I didn't check whether they were processed. Our duty was to apprehend them and refer them to the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, I'm amazed that no Defence intervenes. You have concluded, from the sentence "no previous convictions," that the persons concerned had not been prosecuted. These are two different matters. They may well have been prosecuted and acquitted, or the prosecution may have been stayed for lack of evidence, or whatever. So I think you should be careful not to overdo it in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The reason there was no reaction, at least on this part, is that the presumption of innocence and the burden of proof, and that's why. So merely posing a question, in and of itself, is no proof at all. And there was a presumption on their part, but I agree with you, Your Honour. Perhaps we would be more vigorous, in the future, with our objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I was in no way criticising counsel. My surprise is not based on the theoretical issue, but on previous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Anyway, can we conclude, at least, that these people were not convicted for the crime of rape against these Muslim women, from this document, convicted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, again. At this point we don't know at what stage the proceedings are. We can conclude a lot of things. One of them is that we don't know. Now, if they're able to show that there was a trial and that there was some sort of resolution and that after that resolution we have this document, fine, but we can't jump to any conclusions. We know -- all we can do is speculate, and this individual has already indicated what his role is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you are going farther than I can go along, because here it says "no previous convictions," so we can assume, I think, as this is a judgement, that in the moment this judgement is rendered, there has not yet been a conviction for rape. Maybe it came later, but so far I think no criticism is justified. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to object. The witness, himself, said that he doesn't know anything about the work of the courts; he didn't know what happened to those perpetrators after they had been handed over to the Prosecutor's Office, who was then supposed to issue an indictment. The witness that we have before us is not one who issues indictments, or prosecutes, or deals with court proceedings. He could only tell us what happened to them if he knew them personally. He, himself, says that he didn't know anything, and we shouldn't ask him to speculate. That was not part of his remit, so there's no foundation for this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we support that entirely. It's either no conclusion can be drawn or conclusions can be drawn which don't need the slightest help from this witness. The Trial Chamber can read the document, as Mr. Coric's counsel said. This witness can add absolutely nothing. It's a pointless question to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this document was shown in direct, and I just don't want to have the wrong conclusions be drawn from that document, and that's why I put this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's still a matter of argument and not a matter on which the witness can help at all. If something wrong has come out that the Prosecution say on direct examination, well, they can argue that in due course, but they can't just ask a witness a question on something of which he can offer nothing of any value. That's just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] In the examination-in-chief -- just a moment, please. In the examination-in-chief, the witness was asked whether he knew whether those persons had been arrested and whether criminal charges were filed by the military police against them. And to that, he answered that they were, indeed, arrested and that criminal charges were raised -- or a criminal report was filed against them, and he repeated that today. He didn't say, on examination-in-chief, whether they were convicted or not. I didn't ask him that, because I know that my witness is not a member of the Prosecutor's Office or a member of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, we will proceed, but I believe it would have been much simpler, given all the investigators that you have at hand, to check with the case number of the Military Court of Livno to check what proceedings were pending, because we have the number 1676. By checking those K numbers, you could have been able to check whether criminal proceedings had been instigated against rape charges. And in that case, it would have been extremely simple. But I'm aware that you have a lot of work and that it is sometimes difficult to reach perfection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Colonel, let's move to Prozor. You gave some evidence about Prozor, October 1992. You testified that you were actually in the town of Prozor on the 23rd of October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it correct that armed clashes between the Muslims and Croats broke out on the 23rd of October and that they lasted for about a day and that afterwards the HVO troops took control over the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fighting lasted two days, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to go to Exhibit P00744. And what I would like to discuss with you is the period after the conflict had died down and when the HVO troops actually moved into Prozor town. Now, this document, Colonel, is a document from the Executive Board of the Prozor SDA, and it describes the situation in Prozor once the HVO troops had taken control over the town. And let me read out a part of that document. This is under item number 3, which I'm going to read out: "After the Croat forces had entered the town, a real drama began for those civilians. "4: After those forces had entered the town, some 10 civilians were killed. Women, children, and elderly persons were brought to the location near the buildings of the Ministry of Interior and units taken to assembly camps in the area of Gornja Rama. All other Muslims were arrested and brought in for interrogation. All this lasted for five or six days." Skipping a paragraph, again continuing: "Violence, general insecurity for Muslims, and all that goes with it, did not allow any normalisation of relations. During all that time, the said Muslim citizens were subject to ruthless plundering. It is impossible to describe the quantity of hatred that was discharged on everything that was Muslim in this town. Is it possible that such vandalism occurs at the end of the 20th century? "Almost all Muslim apartments were broken into and looted. All small businesses facilities owned by Muslims were set on fire and destroyed. Croats took almost all cars of all types. Several respected Muslim intellectuals were arrested and kept in prison. We still worry about their fate, for we don't know where they are." Sir, in your evidence you say that crimes were committed but it was only the HOS troops. Are you saying that whatever is described here was all due to the conduct of the HOS units in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons wearing uniforms also bore insignia "HOS," but as I've already told you, that doesn't mean that they had to really belong to HOS. I don't think they were the only ones who caused problems in Prozor. What you have just read out now, I can tell you that it is only partially true, where it says that when the Croatian forces entered the city, a real drama started. And that is simply not true. What Croatian forces? The author of this text, what does he mean when he says "the Croatian forces"? Who does he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You're saying that it may not have been only the HOS troops. What other kinds of units would have been involved in this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe elements of the Rama Brigade, people who were causing havoc and were responsible for the crimes. But as I have just told you, where I was, I did see those men with the HOS insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move to another exhibit, which is P007 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you know - I'm sure you were told - we heard victims who testified here before the Chamber, and they confirmed what is stated in the document, i.e., that they were detained in the Unis building, et cetera, et cetera. I won't go into details here. You've just told us that this document is partially true. I can see that at the end of the document the Prozor SDA seems to have adopted a measured attitude, because they're talking about mixed units, with participation of international forces, to secure the municipality. In other words, it seems that he does not reject the entire responsibility on the HVO, since he's calling for mixed units to be deployed. Now, something seems important to me. Where were you, yourself, during those two days? Physically, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was in the city centre, and I co-ordinated with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You were in the city centre. Did you know that Muslims had been taken and brought to the Unis building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard that they did, and this was done by members of the Rama Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, very well. So members from the Rama Brigade. Now, did you know, as this document states, that interviews were carried out? Because we heard some witnesses saying that they had been interviewed or interrogated. Did you know that such interrogations had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't know that there were interrogations, but it is logical for somebody to inquire as to why the conflict had happened if they believed that that person had been involved actively in that conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question, not to use up the Prosecution's time. Who was carrying out those interrogations, the military police or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the interrogations were carried out by the SIS of the Rama Brigade. Perhaps somebody from the MUP, but I wouldn't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One minor detail. It may not be of interest - I'm not sure - but when I see a document, I look at the entire document. It seems that over those two days, 1500 shells dropped. This is a huge number, 1500. But according to the SDA document, there wouldn't have been any major damage. How do you account for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't know that so many shells had been fired. If 1500 shells had been fired, the city would have disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, my apologies for using some of your time, but, of course, this will not be deducted from the time that's been allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to move to another document, which is P00721. I think you may have already been there. This is, in fact, a report from the SIS in Prozor about what was happening in Prozor town in October 1992. And let me read out to you what the SIS report is. It's P00721, so at the beginning of the binder. This is a SIS report dated the 8th of November, 1992, "Report on the situation in the town following the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH." Let's start reading from the second paragraph: "This conflict, although it was a brief one, has resulted in something that usually occurs in every war - war profiteers saw their opportunity and they took it. "Large-scale thefts of both private and community properties have taken place, including goods, vehicles, and even arms. "The military police have done nothing in that respect, neither have it issued receipts on seized items, which enabled a certain number of military police to take possession of the seized items and arms. "For the aforementioned reasons, the command is working on appointing a new military police commander." Now, sir, here the SIS is actually saying that even military policemen were seizing items and arms, actually took possession of these items; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was issued on the 8th of November, a few days after the conflict. It is possible that some of the military policemen were also engaged in wrong-doings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it not true that you and your units also participated in the plunder of goods belonging to the Muslims and that you took a number of these goods with you to Livno?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is not correct. The unit under my command was in the territory of Prozor for two or three days during the conflict, itself, and then what was left behind was just one company that was deployed in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at Exhibit P00648, please. Now, sir, this is a report from Colonel Siljeg, addressed to the HVO Main Staff, the HVO Military Police Administration, and the Defence Department, and it's an interim report and request to take measures. This is what it reads: "On 25th October, 1992, a part of the military police unit from Livno and Tomislavgrad, under the command of Zdenko Andabak, which was in Prozor, returned to Livno and Tomislavgrad with about 30 illegally-seized motor vehicles, and there are most likely other stolen things. "Motor vehicles range from cars to buses. "Military police commander from Livno told me that Andabak had approved all that. "According to the report by the HVO Rama Brigade commander, Andabak is no longer in Prozor, and there are indications that the houses and property in possession of the Croats was looted." Now, sir, isn't it correct that this report from Siljeg alleges that you actually left Prozor with 30 illegally-seized vehicles? What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this were true, I would have been arrested and processed, I'm sure. This is a lie uttered by the commander of the North-West Herzegovina OG [as interpreted]. The military police went to Jajce before the conflict in Prozor. We did not have the bus which is mentioned here. Actually, we did have a bus, a Livno Autobus bus. And 120 to 130 men travelled either on buses or personal vehicles, and those were all the vehicles that belonged to those units. Somebody gave a false report to Commander Siljeg. It is true that we did have a few vehicles that had been seized from other persons in the town of Prozor after the conflict, and those vehicles were subsequently returned to their rightful owners either in Jablanica, if they had fled to Jablanica, or in Prozor, if they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, sir, if I understand your question [sic] correctly, you say that this is all a lie. Let's read the last paragraph of this document signed by Siljeg. It says: "I require the head of the Military Police Administration to inspect urgently military police units in Livno and Tomislavgrad, consider the situation, and take appropriate measures against individuals who behave like that." Sir, was there a follow-up by Mr. Coric, based on what's in this document ordered by Siljeg? Did Mr. Coric follow up on this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I can remember, the chief of the Military Police Administration didn't appear in person, but some commission was formed that consisted of officers who worked with the military police. We made a list of the cars that we had brought and the cars that had been returned to the owners, so certain measures were taken on the basis of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 3D00424.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'd like to spend a few minutes on this document. This document could be quite overwhelming, because it states that some 30 vehicles were illegally seized. Colonel Siljeg, in this document, says that it is the commander of the Livno military police who told him that you approved all that. In other words, you are questioned -- or your attitude is questioned by the commander of the Livno military police. And Mr. Siljeg reports all these facts and asks for an inspection to be carried out. Why would the Livno military police commander want to put your behaviour into question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the commander of the MP wasn't even carrying out a task in Prozor -- or in the direction of Jajce, rather, so he couldn't have provided him with information as to who had authorised what. I know where the information arrived from. When leaving Prozor, another military formation was entering the area. Their security officers were on good terms with Siljeg, and they told him that the military police was fleeing from the area, that they had stolen cars and buses, all the cars and buses, without being aware of the fact that this was the property of the military police. They didn't know what our real role was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at Exhibit 3D00424. It's in the back of the binder. Now, sir, this is an order from Valentin Coric, co-signed by General Praljak, dated the 14th of November, 1992, and it seems to be a follow-up on what I just read out in that last paragraph from the Siljeg order. Let's read out what this order says: "All vehicles that have been taken away by the HVO military police in Prozor municipality are now located at the stations of the 2nd MP Battalion, must be transported in an organised manner and handed over to the General and Traffic Military Police Section in Ljubuski, to the deputy chief of the General and Traffic Military Police, Ante Alilovic, who will return the vehicles to their owners. "This order must be implemented by 1200 hours on 17 November 1992. The commander of the 2nd Battalion, Zdenko Andabak, and deputy chief of the General and Traffic Military Police, Alilovic, are responsible for carrying out this order." So, sir, do you recall this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do remember the order, and these vehicles were returned to their owners, to those who had contacted us from Jablanica and some from Prozor. There were four or five vehicles in question, but they were vehicles we had taken from third parties. I'll repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Are you saying it was four or five vehicles or twenty vehicles? Because in other documents there was talk about twenty vehicles and not four or five vehicles.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know nothing about 20 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's what we read in one of the other reports, that it was -- that we were talking about. The SIS report stated about 20 vehicles. But, anyway, sir, was anybody punished for this, for the fact that these vehicles were illegally seized from Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let me repeat this. Those vehicles were taken by the MP at check-points after a conflict. They were taken from soldiers who had seized those vehicles. We then took them away with us to guard them and then returned them to their owners. So everyone knew about the four or five vehicles in our possession. Therefore, no one stole any vehicles and, as a result, couldn't be punished for such an act. They kept -- we kept these vehicles in a car park until the time that they were returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm a bit surprised. You always provide explanations at the last minute. Why didn't you say so earlier on when Mr. Bos started asking questions to you? Why didn't you say, Out of the 30 vehicles, I must tell you that some 4 or 5 of them, I can't remember, had been taken by my soldiers, my men, because the drivers of such vehicles had robbed them, and therefore we took such vehicles to keep them and to return them to their lawful owners? Why didn't you say so at the very beginning? Why did you wait until the end to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I answered the questions put to me by the Prosecutor, and later, I said, when the second or third question was put to me, what I knew, what was at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question: Did you, yourself, write a report on those events, with details, in which you explained what had happened, why you had seized the vehicles, to whom they were returned, and so on and so forth? Did you actually draft a report, or an Official Note, because for me it's the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this certainly is a report that mentions the type of car, the make, where it was seized; and on the basis of that report, those vehicles were certainly returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, let's move to Gornji Vakuf, January 1993. On Monday, you were shown a report from Mr. Coric, dated the 5th of January, in which he informed Mr. Bruno Stojic on the deployment of MP troops in the area of Gornji Vakuf. Do you recall that document? It was document P01053, and I want to -- want you to go to that document. But do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you were shown that document, you stated that one of the reasons why the military police was deployed in that region was because there were increasing tensions between the Muslims and the Croats in the region, and one of the reasons why these tensions were increasing was, according to you, that there were ABiH units moving from outside Gornji Vakuf into Gornji Vakuf; isn't that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to look at Exhibit 5D028 -- 2078, 5D02078. Sir, this is a report from the Rama Brigade assistant commander, Petrovic, dated the 6th of December, 1992, and the document actually discusses the intention of the Rama Brigade commander, Ilija Franjic, to resign. And then it's something that we also discussed on Monday. Do you recall that evidence? Now, sir, what I am interested in is the last paragraph of this report. It reads: "Disgusted by this act and the conduct of the injured party's relatives towards him, the commander of the Rama Brigade, Mr. Ilija Franjic, wants to resign the position that he currently holds. He has informed Colonel Siljeg of his intentions. Considering the situation in which we find ourselves and the preparations for offensive operations, I find this request impulsive and unacceptable, and consequently suggest that it be denied." So, sir, there's talk here about preparations for offensive operations in Prozor. What kind of preparations is Mr. Petrovic talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know. This is a brigade document, and the military police wasn't familiar with the activities of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that in December 1992, the HVO was preparing for a large offensive operation into Gornji Vakuf, and that Prozor was the bases where these units prepared for this offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, you are absolutely right. We'll take our last break for the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Bos, the Registrar has told me that you've used 32 minutes of your time, which means that you have an hour and 28 minutes left. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, each of Your Honours -- or I guess afternoon. Sorry, good afternoon, my apologies - and to all those in and around the courtroom. Just one procedural matter, before the day gets away from us, Mr. President. As you know, a number of parties have filed their IC list concerning Mr. Petkovic's testimony. The Prosecution will be filing its list, of course, later today. It's close to being completed. Because of the number of different filings and the number of documents involved, I've spoken to Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Stewart during the one of the breaks, and we propose an agreement, there's no objection, if the Chamber agrees, that the parties would have until close of business next Wednesday to file their various objections to the various filings, if that's agreeable to the Chamber, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber conferred, and we give you until next Wednesday for your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Colonel, we left off before the break in Gornji Vakuf, and I want to continue a little more on that. And I would like you to look at an exhibit that's been shown to you also today and on Monday, which is P01350. P01350. If you could find it in the binder. It's the minutes of the meeting where General Praljak and Mr. Valentin Coric were also present, dated the 27th of January, 1993. 1350. No, you're too far back. It's P1350. Maybe the usher can assist you. So, as I said, these are the minutes, and we've looked at this document on a number of couple of occasions today and on Monday. And I want to read out two parts of these minutes and ask you a couple of questions about it. First is, in the B/C/S version, it's for you, on the second page, the top of the second page, and I'll read it out: "Lavric said that Gornji Vakuf had been a great test for the military police, where they had shown their quality, and that it should be the basis for reorganising and forming MP units. The MP has an assault force which is respected, it can be ranked with a professional army, although they lack the same MTS as the others." Now, sir, Mr. Lavric here is saying that Gornji Vakuf had been a great test for the military police. What did he mean by that? Why was it a great test for the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let's say the military police was one of the forces involved in the defence of the area of Gornji Vakuf, and apart from combat tasks, it also carried out its regular police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that after January 1993, there was the formation of the military police light assault battalions? Was that -- were these created after the Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think the light assault units were formed in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, were, after January 1993, the light assault battalions extensively used in combat operations throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think they were used exclusively for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And "exclusively," so meaning that throughout 1993 these units were operating in the Herceg-Bosna area in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say "exclusively," well, that was their main task, but in 1993 they were also used to bring in certain individuals, criminal -- members of criminal groups. They were used to establish certain check-points where members of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion were needed, but they were used in commands of the operative zones where they were active to engage in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at another part of the minutes. Moving up a bit, going back to page 1 of the minutes, it says: "Mr. Tolj stressed the success of the team led by M. Jelic, but also the problem of the poor state of VP equipment levels and the tasks they were given (mopping up the terrain and guarding positions) compared to other units." Sir, reference here is being made "by M. Jelic." Would that have been Mr. Zlatan Mijo Jevic, the commander of the Active-Duty Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, the person in question is Zlatan Mijo Jelic, but in this document Zlatan Mijo Jelic was then the commander of the 1st Active-Duty Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, sir, it says here the task they were given was mopping up the terrain and guarding positions. What is meant by "mopping up the terrain"?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not aware of them having had activities of any other kind apart from holding the positions reached, so I'm not aware of the fact that they were involved in mopping-up operations. All I know is that they held their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you were not involved in mopping-up operations when you were in Gornji Vakuf? Mr. Jelic may have been, but you weren't; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I know this for certain: The positions reached were guarded. I know that Mr. Jelic did that too. He had no other activities that involved mopping up the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to look at P01330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Colonel, we are looking again at a document that we've seen on numerous occasions. It's document P1350, which is a Prosecution's document. You were there at that meeting, and I notice that this meeting took quite a long time, about three hours and forty-five minutes, if I'm correct. And I was struck by the conclusion of the meeting, which is of a political nature. As far as you can recollect, who came up with this conclusion? Look at the last four lines of the document. You said that you were fighting for Croat cantons, but you have actually lost more than you have gained in Geneva. You have to respect the feelings of every Muslim in your ranks, and you will not fire on your own people. And co-operation has to happen at all levels. Who has drawn this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I think all of us who attended the meeting discussed matters in a general way. This was a conclusion according to which we should protect areas inhabited by Croats. So all the participants took the floor. That's why the meeting lasted for such a long time. And among other things, these are the conclusions that were reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you do not know who specifically drew the conclusion? You have say that everyone really contributed; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bos, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If we are -- excuse me. If I may just add a question. In this passage referred to by the President, it is said: "Muslims need to know what we are fighting for. Croatian cantons are a reality, but also a compromise. We lost more than we gained at Geneva." This could be read as meaning that what you are fighting for are Croatian cantons as a reality and a compromise. Is that a correct reading of this text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to look at Exhibit P01330. Sir, this is a report from the 3rd Brigade, Defence Department -- the SIS, 3rd Brigade, Defence Department, dated the 27th of January, 1993. And I would just like you to read out -- I'll just read out the last part of the report, which reads as follows: "Two villages with exclusively Muslim population were burned on the right side of the road. These villages were burned by members of the HVO military police. According to unverified information, their commander was Mijo-Zlatan Jelic, from Siroki Brijeg." Sir, would this have been the Mijo Jevic which you've just confirmed was also in Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I apologise, my learned friend, but "according to verified information," was the information we received, whereas it says "according to unverified information," so that's why I got to my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It does read "unverified information," that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, sir, is this the Zlatan Mijo Jevic which you just said was in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, that's the same man, Zlatan Mijo Jevic. But this unverified information and all of this, well, I know where Zlatan Mijo Jevic was. He couldn't have entered Gornji Vakuf, because before Gornji Vakuf, at the Karamustafic check-point, he needed to turn right three kilometres ahead to go to that village, so there's no question of the military police being there at all, whereas he mentions an MP unit. So for him to arrive at that village, he had to turn off the road three kilometres before the check-point and before Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you seem to be saying that you knew about which village this report is talking about. I don't see that the name of the village is identified. It simply says "these villages were burned." Would you know the name of these villages?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic held a position which was called "baba," and that's above the village of Zdrimci. So here what is referred to is the entrance to Gornji Vakuf, which is where he was not, he wasn't there. They are two other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any indication that Mr. Jelic will not, in fact, turn left or turn right where he had to turn right to get to the villages? I mean, it's not really an argument to say he would have turned off -- if he wanted to go that way, he would have turned off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mijo Jelic, when he reported to the forward command post at Prozor with his unit, he was given a local scout or escort from the area who guided him. And I know that because I went that way too. There's no other route. Otherwise, he would have reached the Bosniak check-point and fallen into Bosniak hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified that Valentin Coric -- during this operation in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, that Valentin Coric was not in the country and that he, in fact, was in Zagreb; is that correct? And I think you've said that he was hospitalised in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, that is correct, and that's what I said. I know for sure he wasn't there during all the events in Gornji Vakuf, that he arrived only prior to the meeting that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In your view, when you were in Gornji Vakuf, was he still the commander for you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Coric wasn't the commander. He was chief of the MP Administration. He was the chief, the head. And in his absence, his deputy would take over, Mr. Lakic [phoen], who performed the duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at P01134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Colonel, before we move to the next document. Sometimes I'm surprised by the content of documents. Where it says that parts of the HVO are denouncing each other, basically, and I could, and I'm using the conditional here, I could reach the conclusion that no one really agreed, that there was not really any plan. Because when you look at this document, the SIS, which is part of the HVO, until proven wrong, that's the situation. And in this document it says that members of the military police under the command of Mr. Jelic burned down houses. So, in a way, they are implicated in this matter. So how do you explain that? Within the HVO, some people are actually reporting acts that were committed by others. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, as we would say, I want the problems that I have to be dealt with by others, and so this commander of the 3rd Brigade, for instance -- or, rather, the SIS officer in question was supposed to cover his brigade. He had nothing to do with the military police, and that's the problem. The fact that they did very little work, they accused and shifted the blame on to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is your take on events. Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this isn't my time for examination, but perhaps it would be useful if someone were to ask the witness what operative zone does the 3rd Brigade belong to and whether the 3rd Brigade was in Gornji Vakuf at all. Let's start out from there so that we don't misunderstand this and think that reference made here is to a local brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're very right. I should have thought of it, and I didn't. I was wondering what Operational Zone the SIS and the 3rd Brigade are covering mainly. Can you answer this question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SIS and the 3rd Brigade -- now, was it Central Bosnia or -- I don't know which 3rd Brigade is referred to. The first was in North-West Herzegovina, the other one was in South-East Herzegovina, and the third was, I think, in Central Bosnia, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does this mean to say that the SIS, reporting on what is happening in Gornji Vakuf, did not have a "ration illusi" [phoen] competence to intervene in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they did have the competence to and the authority to report information and collect information about units and what they were doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but might I be of assistance? In your question, it says "whether SIS." It's not a question of SIS here in the document, it's a question of the 3rd Brigade, because the Prosecutor said this in his question and the witness repeated that it was SIS within the 3rd Brigade. From your question, one might conclude that you had something general in mind, whereas this is the SIS of the 3rd Brigade. So may that be recorded in very precise terms in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for me it's very clear. It's the SIS of the 3rd Brigade, of course. So now I was wondering whether the 3rd Brigade had, for area of competence, Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd Brigade did not have authority -- or, rather, most probably it was attached for carrying out assignments in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: One follow-up question on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, isn't it correct that HVO units from outside Gornji Vakuf were also involved in this operation; that it was just not the local units that were involved in this operation, but also units from outside, including the military police from Livno?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes. And units which were not from the Gornji Vakuf area, they took part in operations too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could it be that the 3rd Brigade, for that reason, was also involved in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it most probably was involved because of the lack of manpower or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, I had asked you to look at Exhibit P01134, which is an order from Valentin Coric, dated the 14th of January, 1993. So this is at the time that the operations in Gornji Vakuf were ongoing. And it says: "Due to the arisen security situation caused by the attack of the units of the Army of BiH against the units of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf, I herewith order: "The total blockade of the border-crossings towards the Republic of Croatia for vehicles, cargo, and members of the Army of BiH." And then it continues and it ends: "I charge the commander of the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion, as barer, and the commanders of the traffic platoons of the 2nd and 3rd Battalions of the Military Police with the duty to carry out this order. The commanders from the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Battalions of the Military Police, and the officers from the Department of the Main and Traffic Military Police, shall supervise the carrying out of this order." And then the document is CC'd to all these commanders and also to the commanders of the Operational Zone of South-East Herzegovina and North-West Herzegovina. Sir, now the document is -- and Valentin Coric's name is underneath there, and it's true that the document wasn't signed by Mr. Valentin Coric, but by somebody else for Valentin Coric. But wouldn't you agree that such a big and important order would have been an order that at least would have been approved by Mr. Valentin Coric, if not also drafted by Mr. Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Coric certainly never wrote an order of this kind. This order, once again, came from somewhere, and the person signing it could not have issued this order independently. It must have come from some higher level. And I know for sure that he didn't write it, nor did he authorise it, because he wasn't there. But his deputy was authorised to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that even though that "Mr. Valentin Coric" is underneath this order, that he would not have known about this order? It's a very important order, I'd say. Are you suggesting that this was made up by somebody else within the military police, without Mr. Valentin Coric knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that's quite certain. I do believe that Mr. Coric never knew about this. If he went off for treatment, then it was the person who was responsible and authorised could sign. Rade Lavric couldn't call up Coric every time he needed to do something, to execute something. When I was absent, my deputy would take my place, act for me. So I am certain, and I'm telling you that, that he didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't understand how you could be so certain that he didn't know about it. Mr. Coric was in hospital in Zagreb. Now, surely they must have been able to communicate with Mr. Coric in Zagreb, and how are you -- how can you be so certain that Mr. Coric didn't know anything about this very important order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know how the system functioned, who replaces whom and acts as deputy for whom, and why, and who had what authority. And, as I say, if I received an order, let's take that example, me, as a battalion commander, to send the battalion somewhere, and I wasn't there, I was absent, then my deputy would go ahead because he has permission from me and authority to move the troops, move the battalion. So if you're the Prosecutor and you're taken ill, for example, somebody calls you up and asks you to what -- to ask me what the situation was like, Mr. Coric could have done that. But I'm sure he didn't write this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, sir, you have orders and orders. And, you know, if it's not such an important order, I can understand. But here we're talking about a main order addressed to all the commanders of all the battalions operating in Gornji Vakuf. It also goes to the commanders of the Operational Zone of the South-East Herzegovina and the North-West Herzegovina, and are you saying, Well, Mr. Rade Lavric could have issued this order, being the deputy of Mr. Coric and replacing Mr. Coric, without Mr. Coric knowing about this order? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my evidence. But Rade Lavric didn't write this order alone, either. It came from somewhere, from some instance. Whether from the ministry or where, it doesn't refer to it. But he couldn't have taken this decision on his own, either, independently. So somebody ordered him to write this, but I know for certain that that person wasn't Valentin Coric. He just carried out the order he received, and I mean specifically Lavric when I say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this is an issue that we already discussed in this courtroom, and it may not be entirely clear for everyone. Let me take an example. Imagine that you, yourself -- imagine that you have to go to hospital in Zagreb. How will it work within the 2nd Battalion? What are you going to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would inform the commander of the operative zone in my absence to -- that my deputy would be replacing me and that he would resolve and carry out all tasks linked to the operative zone, the Military Police Administration -- linked to the Military Police Administration, and so on, and that he has the authority to sign documents and to implement those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's the way it had to work within the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We'll leave the topic and we'll move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that after Gornji Vakuf, the operations in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, that you and your units were -- from Livno were involved in combat operations in Konjic and Jablanica in April 1993, around mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, since Jablanica and Konjic were under the North-Western Herzegovina Operative Zone, we had parts -- I don't know what operations you mean in Jablanica and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe we'll clarify. Let's look at Exhibit P02202, and then things may be clarified. This is another document that was also shown to you by the Petkovic Defence. It's an interim report on the violations of law and order in Livno on 4th of May, and it's signed by you, and it's addressed to Mr. Boban, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Coric. Now, sir, it seems to me a bit out of the ordinary for you to draft a report to all these high-level people. Had you been ordered to submit this report, or could you give me the background for why this report was issued?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, I'll readily answer your question. The interim report came into being with respect to the local brigade's relationship towards the military police. It was duty-bound to supply the military police with MTS, that is to say, ammunition, equip -- uniforms, and so on, and its activities in Livno. And when coming back from an area of that kind, the military police would park in Livno, at the bus stop there. There was a bit of shooting, and then they went home.
